mentions.excerpt: Ren puts the commercial point cleanly: Bloom is not selling electrons; it is selling time-to-power.
In Ren’s account, Bloom got Oracle running in 55 days.
This is why Ren’s ranking matters.
Ren, who remains fully invested in the AI trade, says a 10-year yield near 5% is the hurdle every long-duration growth company must clear.
Ren points to the income statements: Azure grew 43%, Google Cloud 82% and AWS 37%, its fastest pace in eighteen quarters.
Ren sees more capable models creating more agents, longer tasks and recurring inference demand.
Ren, who follows the AI stack layer by layer, describes the economic shift: once software researches, chooses, executes and pays, it sits between shopper and seller.
“The unit of work is moving from the prompt to the objective,” Ren writes.
Ren says the cost of an error rises when software acts: a wrong chatbot answer costs a minute, while an agent can rebook a flight.
Ren looked at the same arithmetic on October 5 and titled a portfolio update “The Cheapest ‘Bubble’ I’ve Ever Seen.”
Ren says profits carried the rally.
Ren warns that chip designs turn over faster than factories can be rebuilt; this year’s winning server could be beaten within five years.

sides.claim: AI data center buildout is bottlenecked by power delivery, not compute, since compute can be ordered faster than power can be delivered to a site.
Bloom's real product is time-to-power rather than electrons, because stranding a multi-billion-dollar GPU cluster for 18-24 months costs far more than paying a premium for onsite electricity.
